title: I Enforced the Vinyl-Cutter Roll Log on the Chair Whose Nephew Cut My Film

parts.text: I stepped into cutter bay at 1:04 p.m. and chair Mara was already using my numbered film. The board said: ONE ROLL. FORTY MINUTES. FILM STAYS WITH THE BOOKING. I was thirty-two, sign-shop steward, holding a clipboard that listed our weeding. Mara shrugged. "Family is the shop." I photographed the board, the booking, and her nephew on my roll. Then I asked for the roll log. At 1:12 the sign desk pinged why Mara's nephew sat on our roll. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The sign desk can see Mara's nephew on the cutter during our weeding.

social.video_title: Her nephew cut my numbered vinyl roll — Part 1/2
social.description: Vinyl cutter, a nephew on my roll, a forty-minute clock she posted. I logged the film. Would you have asked for the roll log?

parts.text: Mara called it practice weeding until the desk asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the roll still. The film went back to my numbered core. Mara ran a slot of their own and told the next chair atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: FAMILY IS NOT THE SHOP. I keep our weeding on a labeled card. Mara brown-bags nephew hours. The cutter finally looks like a booking, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Family is not the shop — Part 2/2
social.description: Roll log, numbered film, and a second line on the board. Was practice weeding ever our film?
